$note: Port type registration rules, graded by the backend's PortTypeWideningTable
(dotnet/tests/ReeveWorkflow.Core.Tests/Compilation/PortTypeRegistrationCorpusTests.cs): 'backend' is the verdict of each row.
The editor's createPortTypeRegistry (packages/core/src/portTypes/registrationCorpus.test.ts) reads the records the backend accepts,
the 'term' rows and the capabilities section. It grades no other rule of a record: it refuses only a name that does not parse, a key
two entries claim and an allowed argument that is not a term. The registration holds no port relations (TypeFrom).
alias: the backend runs Builtin.WithAlias(alias, target); the editor reads the builtins with the alias
added to the target's definition, or a new definition named target with that alias.
assignable: IsAssignable on Builtin; the editor has no assignability.
backendRefusal: what a refused registration's error says, a pattern on the backend's message; for a term row, the 'code: message' the registry's refusalOf answers too.
widening: the backend runs Builtin.With(from, widensTo); the editor reads the builtins plus a definition named
from with that widensTo, or adds it to the builtin's own. declare: Builtin.Declaring(type); the editor, a definition
named type. A collection widens through its element, so neither half registers a row from or onto one. An alias
onto a collection name is one both halves hold at any depth, as Builtin.WithAlias's target and this editor's
collection-shaped definition, whose atom is declared at no other depth.
constructor: a host constructor record {head, allowedArguments} registered on the builtins plus this row's declaredAtoms (atoms) and
after (constructor records registered first, in order). The backend runs WorkflowTypeConstructorRecord through PortTypeWideningTable.WithConstructor;
the editor passes it to createPortTypeRegistry. A refusal is named by code: port-type-registration-invalid for the record, port-type-name-clash for a name taken.
term: whether a closed document term is registered under termVocabulary (its declared atoms and constructor records): accepts when every head and
atom is registered and every constructor argument is one of the head's allowed arguments (an exact term, nullable or not), refuses with
port-type-unregistered otherwise. The backend asks PortTypeWideningTable.RefusalOf, the editor registry.refusalOf; a refusal is read as 'code: message'.
alias, widening and declare rows may carry constructors (records registered first): the type or alias is then the thing refused. A constructor row may declare
declaredWidenings [{from, widensTo}] and declaredAliases [{alias, target}] before it registers; a widening target counts as registered.
Any and Float are not port types: the declare, alias and widening rows naming either are refused by the backend's table API with port-type-alias, and a value of either feeds nothing.
row: the backend registers WorkflowTypeRecords (the declared atoms and aliases, then 'from' with widensTo) in a WorkflowTypeRegistry and expects a WorkflowTypeRegistrationException;

the editor reads an accepted row's definitions and constructors through createPortTypeRegistry. A row's target is a registered plain name or a closed term of a registered constructor, spelled canonically;
a collection term is never a target, and one atom has one row into any one constructor head. A row whose target later leaves the registry is dormant, which only the registry tests grade.
A row target, like a constructor's allowed argument, must be owned by the library, the host or the record's own owner; the reference rows grade that on the backend.
A record named Any or Float, an alias spelled either and a row naming either are refused here with port-type-registration-invalid, the code a refused record gets.
capabilities (written by hand, never generated): the backend builds a WorkflowTypeRegistry from vocabulary

(a CLR type, JsonTypeInfo and Sample that make each claim true) and grades all of it; the editor builds a createPortTypeRegistry and grades capabilities, the vectors' implements and refused through implementsCapability.

capabilities: the closed vocabulary as GET port-types publishes it, in this order. constraints: the names a type parameter may be constrained by (Iterable is not one: the associated-type form is not offered). hostClaimable: what a host record may claim.
vectors: a closed term and every capability it implements, in vocabulary order; item is the Item of Iterable<Item> and is absent when the term is not Iterable.
A nullable term implements JsonSerializable when its non-null term does, and nothing else. Collection<T> is Iterable<Item=T>, Equatable iff T is, JsonSerializable iff T is.

For every vector the backend also asserts that the term is assignable to Json (to Json? when the term is nullable) exactly when it implements JsonSerializable: rule A4 (docs/reference/port-types.md, Widening and assignability) reads the same claims.
refused: terms that name something the vocabulary does not register (an unknown name, an argument outside a constructor's allowed arguments, Any, Float): membership is not answered for them;
implementsCapability refuses each with port-type-unregistered in both halves, so a caller grades registration (refusalOf) first.

claim: a host record {subject: atom or constructor, head, clr, claims} registered on its own. clr names the CLR type the backend gives the record (string, guid, memoryStream or object); a claim of JsonSerializable

gets the JsonTypeInfo of that type, and jsonTypeInfoOf: "string" gives the record the string's instead; the editor has no CLR type. A claim of Iterable or Numeric, or of a name that is no capability, is refused with capability-claim-invalid naming the record;
a claim the CLR type does not bear out is refused too. Both are the backend's: the editor reads an accepted claim.
literal: a host record {subject: atom or constructor, head, clr, literal: {gradedAs, format?}} registered on its own, graded by Validate on the backend; the editor reads an accepted form.

A form is graded as one of String, Boolean, Int, Number or Json, and a format (Uuid or DateTime) goes only with String; a member outside the closed set, or a format on another form, is port-type-registration-invalid.
The backend has no name for a member outside its enums and writes its number (99 in these rows). How a literal is graded is contracts/literal-coercion.json.

A claim row may carry jsonTypeInfoOf: "string", the string's JsonTypeInfo on a record whatever it claims; a JsonTypeInfo that describes another type than the record's CLR type is port-type-registration-invalid, claimed or not.
The backend gives a literal row the string's JsonTypeInfo unless the row says jsonTypeInfo: false, and refuses a literal form without one; the editor has no JsonTypeInfo.
reference (references between records): records [{owner, atom | constructorName, allowedArguments?, widensTo?}] registered one at a time in order, each under its owner, in one WorkflowTypeRegistry.

Every record but the last must be accepted; the last is the one the row grades, by 'code (record): message'. The editor has no owner, so it reads an accepted row by registering the same definitions together.
